title: Resilience: Recovery Sites, Diversity, and Redundancy

blocks.text: Resilience is not just "having backups". It answers a specific question: **how does the service continue, and then recover, after an outage or disaster?** The exam expects you to distinguish recovery sites, redundancy, and continuity mechanisms.

The **Defensive Security Handbook** clearly separates the two: business continuity aims at overall business continuation, while disaster recovery refers to the IT processes that achieve the objectives set by continuity.
Do not confuse: **BCP** = keep the organization operating; **DR** = restore systems and data. DR serves BCP.

blocks.field: Fully operational site, data continuously synchronized. Recovery in minutes, highest cost.
Equipment installed and configured, data restored from recent backups. Recovery in hours.
Premises and power only; hardware and data must be installed. Recovery in days, lowest cost.

blocks.text: The three site tiers are **required by the SY0-801 §3.4 objectives**, but none of the four provided books names them explicitly. The definitions above come from the objectives and industry practice, not from book attribution.

**Diversity** reduces the risk that a single failure affects all environments: provider, hardware, virtualization. **Redundancy** eliminates single points of failure via load balancing, clustering, autoscaling, high availability, and multicloud.

blocks.note: Clustered high availability and alternative systems

items: **Load balancing**: distributes load across multiple servers.
**Clustering**: multiple nodes acting as a single service.
**High availability**: redundancy aiming for minimal interruption.
**Multicloud systems**: distributing services across multiple providers.

head: Element
Role
rows: Uninterruptible power supply, short autonomy, bridge time to generator
Redundant power supply within a single device

blocks.text: UPS, RPS, generator, and surge protector are listed in **§3.4 objectives**; no book details them. Memorize as a list.

blocks.q: A site has servers and networking, but data must be restored from the latest backup before restarting. Which site is this?
blocks.explain: A warm site is pre-equipped but requires data restoration. A hot site is continuously synchronized; a cold site also requires hardware installation.

items: BCP = overall continuity; DR = IT restoration.
Hot = minutes, Warm = hours, Cold = days.
Redundancy: load balancing, clustering, autoscaling, HA, multicloud.
Power: UPS, RPS, generator, surge protector.

title: RTO, RPO, MTTR, MTBF, and Recovery Testing

blocks.text: Recovery metrics turn a vague requirement ("we must restore quickly") into a measurable target. They are at the heart of exam scenario questions.

left.title: RPO — Recovery Point Objective
points: Measured in time, before the incident.
A 1-hour RPO requires backups or replication at least hourly.

right.title: RTO — Recovery Time Objective
points: A 1-hour RTO requires a recovery mechanism under one hour.

blocks.note: RPO and RTO definitions, numerical example

blocks.field: Average time required to repair a failed piece of equipment and return it to service.
Average operating time between two failures; measures reliability.

blocks.text: MTTR and MTBF are required in **§3.4**; absent from the four books. Exact magnitudes matter less than the distinction between reliability (MTBF) vs. restoration time (MTTR), which is what is tested.

The book gives a striking example: an email server with a 1-hour RTO on a network whose RTO is 3 hours. The actual RTO of email is therefore **3 hours**: recovery cannot be faster than its slowest element.

items: **Immutability**: unmodifiable copies, even by a compromised administrator account — defense against ransomware.
**Restoration testing**: an untested backup is not a backup.

blocks.text: An immutable backup is often the expected answer when a scenario mentions ransomware encrypting or deleting backups.

items.title: Failover
items.text: Actual switchover to the backup site or system, with named authorities.

items.title: Simulation
items.text: Controlled exercise that validates the procedure without interrupting production.

items.title: Parallel processing
items.text: Simultaneous processing on both sites to compare results.

items.title: Failback
items.text: Return to the primary site once the incident is resolved — often forgotten!

blocks.note: COOP: avoid over-engineering, plan for common occurrences

blocks.q: An outage lasts 4 hours. Data was lost for the last 45 minutes. Which metrics describe this?
blocks.explain: RPO measures data loss (45 min); RTO measures service interruption (4 h). MTTR is the average repair duration, not the duration of this specific incident.

items: RPO = acceptable data loss; RTO = acceptable outage duration.
A recovery chain is only as fast as its slowest link.
Immutability and restoration testing are indispensable.
